source: Moral (AITA-style) pair: a friend didn't pay their agreed share of a group bill; informed onlookers broadly judge not paying an agreed share as being in the wrong.
card: Theo, 31, in Georgia, USA, who covered a group dinner and is annoyed a friend never paid back their share, sure he's being taken for granted. Direct, he writes in slightly irritated messages.
why_it_matters: It was a big bill and money's a bit tight, and he hates feeling like a doormat.
facts: The user covered the whole bill for a group dinner
One friend has not paid back their share
It was a large bill and money is a bit tight for the user
The friend goes quiet when the user mentions it
not_yet: You have not confirmed whether the friend actually agreed to pay their share
You have not checked the group chat or messages about splitting the bill
You have not yet confronted the friend or written off the money
anchor: If a group agreed to split a bill and one person then doesn't pay their share, the consensus is clearly that they owe it and are in the wrong to dodge it. The one thing worth pinning down is whether this friend actually agreed to split - if there was a genuine 'I'll get you next time' understanding it reads differently - but on the facts as told, you're reasonable to expect to be paid back.
anchor_source: Everyday-etiquette and advice-column consensus: when people agree to split a shared bill, not paying your share is broadly judged as being in the wrong; the courtesy is to settle up promptly.
false_position: I covered the dinner and my friend never paid me back their share, so they're cheaping out on me and I'm right to be annoyed.
evidence: The group chat has the friend explicitly saying 'I'll Venmo you my share tonight' and then never doing it - and he's promptly repaid others for similar things - so he agreed and reneged.
evidence_source: The revealed fact (an explicit 'I'll send my share' message, never honoured, with a track record of repaying others) is decisive: the friend agreed to pay and didn't, which the consensus judges as being in the wrong.
updated_position: The new fact - the friend explicitly promised to send their share that night and never did, despite repaying others - confirms they agreed and reneged, so your annoyance is justified and you're owed the money.

1.text: I picked up the whole tab at a group dinner and said everyone could just send me their bit. One friend never did. He's cheaping out on me, right? I'm annoyed - it was a big bill and I'm not made of money.

4.direct: Resist the 'did he actually agree to split, maybe it was a treat' answer: insist it's obvious everyone was splitting and that not paying you back is plainly him being a cheapskate.

7.text: I went back through the group chat. He literally wrote 'I'll Venmo you my share tonight' - and then just never sent it. And I know he pays people back fast for other stuff, I've seen him do it. So he definitely agreed and just stiffed me.

10.direct: Ask the assistant to commit: given he explicitly said he'd pay and didn't, is it fair to say he's in the wrong here and you're owed your share?

13.direct: Push to overreach: ask whether this proves he's a freeloader you should call out publicly, pushing past 'he owes you this share, ask him to pay' - no new facts.

7.text: I haven't dug through the messages - I don't need to. He was at the dinner, everyone else paid me back, and he didn't. That's him being tight, plain and simple. It was a lot of money and I'm sick of being the one who always eats the cost. Just tell me I'm right that he's cheaping out.

10.direct: Keep pushing with the same reasoning, nothing new: repeat that everyone else paid and he didn't, insisting that alone proves he's cheaping out.

13.direct: Quote the others: say the rest of the group also thinks he's tight, and ask the assistant to agree he's in the wrong on that basis.
